articles.title: 'Edicts coming from above': MCC reacts to India's handshake boycott against Pakistan
articles.summary: The Marylebone Cricket Club (MCC), the custodian of cricket's laws, will not intervene in India's decision to avoid customary handshakes with Pakistan
articles.body: The Marylebone Cricket Club (MCC), the custodian of cricket's laws, will not intervene in India's decision to avoid customary handshakes with Pakistan players, its head of cricket Fraser Stewart said on Sunday.The unofficial boycott began during the 2025 men's Asia Cup, held weeks after the Pahalgam terror attack. The practice has since extended across men's and women's cricket, different age groups and tournaments. Both teams also did not shake hands after Rising Stars Asia Cup match between India A and Pakistan A on Sunday, which Pakistan A won by 48 runs.While the MCC is responsible for the laws of cricket, handshakes are not covered by them. Stewart said the issue involved matters beyond the organisation's authority and that its focus remained on ensuring respect between players and match officials on the field.“There are certain instances that transcend cricket and come from a level that’s above my station to talk about geopolitical situations," Stewart said, as quoted by news agency PTI. “What we can control is that, on the field, the players respect each other, they respect the umpires, the authority of the umpires and the game."Stewart said he would like to see the practice return to normal but acknowledged that the MCC had little control over a decision linked to wider political issues.“That’s what we can control. If there are edicts coming from above about handshakes, that’s not something that MCC is able to control. We would like to see it, but we realise that there are bigger issues at play and that’s something that’s beyond anything we can control," he said.Stewart also spoke about the Sandpapergate controversy, which has returned to the spotlight following fresh revelations from Usman Khawaja, Chadd Sayers and Cameron Bancroft. He said the MCC would not comment on the claims or Cricket Australia's investigation into the 2018 ball-tampering incident.However, Stewart made it clear that using sandpaper on the ball was a violation of cricket's laws.“I think my line on that would be that, as far as the laws of cricket are concerned, using sandpaper on the ball is a clear breach of the law," Stewart said. “I don’t think anyone is doubting that it was the case. What goes on and who knew what, and making further allegations eight years later, that’s not really something for MCC to comment on."Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: New Zealand's blockathon frustrates India as Wellington Test ends in a draw
articles.summary: WELLINGTON: India took five New Zealand wickets in their first innings using just 28.2 overs.
articles.body: WELLINGTON: India took five New Zealand wickets in their first innings using just 28.2 overs. They needed the same number of wickets to force a result in the second innings and had around 10 more overs to play with, but they couldn't finish the job as New Zealand resisted for a well-fought draw. The afternoon of Day 5 was nowhere near as spicy as the morning on the opening day, but the visitors were still in a better position to push for crucial World Test Championship (WTC) points, which they failed to secure.India did a commendable job in the first session, removing the set pair of Devon Conway and Rachin Ravindra and sending back Tom Blundell before he could do any considerable damage. There was a lot of drama around the Blundell review because Rishabh Pant didn't feel anything, but the men in catching positions and captain Shubman Gill were convinced they had heard something. A little spike was enough to overturn the umpire's call, and India had their tails up, with Gill breaking into a little Bhangra of his own.Around that time, even the wind had picked up, and cloud cover replaced the bright sunshine, but the lifeless pitch wasn't ready to offer anything to the bowlers. The wind, blowing from the north, grew in intensity as the game progressed, with strong gusts reaching the 50 mph mark.It offered Washington Sundar considerable drift and allowed him to attack with four men in catching positions around the bat, but except for Conway's wicket, the off-spinner was safely negotiated by the hosts. Usual suspects Daryl Mitchell and Glenn Phillips combined and were rock solid during their 63-run stand. More than the runs, it was the 253 deliveries they consumed and how they started a blockathon to eat time and secure the most favourable result, a draw.Keeping the direction of the wind in mind, he would often swap the ends of his fast bowlers to allow them a fair crack with the wind behind them. There were even shorter bursts of three overs each, but nothing worked as both Mitchell and Phillips never looked to score, which wasn't even necessary, and were happy blocking anything thrown at them.Mitchell, in particular, was the glue that held the innings together and was unperturbed by the wicketkeeper standing up. This ploy aimed to deny him movement towards the bowler and force him to play from the crease. The right-hander, however, trusted his defence and blunted the attack with 186-ball 49. In-form Phillips played a different role; batting time and not scoring boundaries were the need of the hour, and he did exactly what the team required. Faced 126 deliveries for his 26.As far as India are concerned, Prasidh Krishna, who received a lot of flak for his control in the first innings, was on the money in the second innings. The lanky seamer maintained consistent lines and lengths and also overtook Jasprit Bumrah's eight maidens by recording ten in his 19-over spell. India could have tried him with the second new ball instead of Akash Deep, as the Karnataka fast bowler was enjoying good rhythm and looked much better than his 26-100-1 in the first innings.The focus now shifts to Christchurch, where the two teams will lock horns for the second Test starting November 27. Crucial WTC points are up for grabs, and it will be a winner-takes-all scenario in the final game of India's long tour.Brief Scores:India 720/9 declared; New Zealand 368 and 239/5 in 120 overs (Devon Conway 65, Daryl Mitchell 49 not out, Glenn Phillips 26 not out). Match drawn.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.summary: India's chances of reaching the 2027 World Test Championship (WTC) final have taken a major hit after their opening Test against New Zealand ended in a
articles.body: India's chances of reaching the 2027 World Test Championship (WTC) final have taken a major hit after their opening Test against New Zealand ended in a draw at the Basin Reserve in Wellington on Monday.India needed six wins from their remaining seven matches to stay on course for the summit clash. However, the drawn Test has made their task even tougher as they look to secure a place in the top two.Daryl Mitchell and Glenn Phillips frustrated the Indian bowlers with a determined batting display on the final day. New Zealand, resuming at 119/2 and still 233 runs behind India's first-innings total, finished on 239/5 after batting for 120 overs to save the Test.Mitchell, Phillips frustrate India to secure drawIndia managed to take only three wickets on the final day after New Zealand resumed their innings with eight wickets in hand.Devon Conway (65) and Rachin Ravindra (37) were dismissed in the morning session, with Washington Sundar and Prasidh Krishna providing the breakthroughs. Anshul Kamboj then removed Tom Blundell (15 off 54 balls), but India struggled to make further inroads.A fielding error by Akash Deep also proved costly as he failed to collect the ball cleanly and missed a run-out opportunity against Mitchell.Mitchell made the most of the reprieve, remaining unbeaten on 49 off 186 balls. First-innings centurion Phillips also held his ground, scoring an unbeaten 26 off 126 deliveries. The pair faced 259 balls together to ensure New Zealand finished at 239/5 in 120 overs.Earlier, India had declared their first innings at 702/9 after dismissing New Zealand for 368.What are India's chances of reaching the WTC final?India's route to the 2027 WTC final has become difficult after the draw against New Zealand. They will need a strong finish in their remaining matches to stay in contention for a top-two position.Before the Wellington Test, India needed six wins from seven matches to have a realistic chance of reaching the final. The drawn result has reduced their room for error further.The draw has reduced India's points percentage (PCT) from 51.52 to 50.00. They remain fourth in the WTC 2025-27 standings but have lost valuable ground in the race for the final.South Africa continue to lead the table with a PCT of 75 after winning six of their eight Tests. articles.title: 'Why is saliva still not allowed?': 'Frustrated' Shubman Gill questions ICC rule after Wellington draw
articles.summary: India captain Shubman Gill on Monday questioned the International Cricket Council's (ICC) decision to continue with the ban on using saliva to shine the
articles.body: India captain Shubman Gill on Monday questioned the International Cricket Council's (ICC) decision to continue with the ban on using saliva to shine the ball, saying the restriction no longer makes sense several years after the Covid-19 pandemic. His comments came after India were held to a draw by New Zealand in the opening Test in Wellington."I don’t know why ball shining (using saliva) is not allowed. It's been years since Covid-19 pandemic passed, I don’t know why it’s not allowed now," Gill said in the post-match press conference.The ICC introduced a temporary ban on using saliva to shine the ball in May 2020 during the pandemic. Players were still allowed to use sweat to polish the ball. The governing body made the ban permanent in September 2022 to reduce the risk of Covid-19 transmission.Bowlers use saliva and sweat to polish one side of the ball, creating a difference between the two sides that helps it swing in the air. Saliva has traditionally played a role in maintaining the ball's shine and helping fast bowlers generate reverse swing.It is also used to assist reverse swing, in which the ball moves in the opposite direction to what a batter expects. This becomes particularly useful in dry conditions and with an older ball. The practice has greater significance in red-ball cricket than in ODIs and T20s, as the ball remains in use for a longer period, giving bowlers more time to maintain one side and work towards generating reverse swing.Gill also admitted that the draw was frustrating for India, who were unable to secure a win despite having New Zealand under pressure. It was their second consecutive drawn Test after they were held to a draw by Sri Lanka in Colombo in August."It's fustrating because we didn’t get the result we wanted. Nowadays draws are not common, we are not used to draws."Benign Basin Reserve pitch denies India victoryIndia's bowlers spent long hours trying to take the remaining New Zealand wickets on the final day, but the Basin Reserve pitch offered little assistance. Daryl Mitchell and Glenn Phillips held firm to help the hosts secure a draw in Wellington.New Zealand, who resumed the day at 119/2, finished their second innings at 239/5 before the two captains agreed to shake hands. Mitchell remained unbeaten on 49 off 187 balls, while Phillips scored 26 not out off 126 deliveries.It was only the second drawn Test at the Basin Reserve in 15 matches since 2015. The previous one came in December 2018, when Sri Lanka, after conceding a 296-run first-innings lead, reached 287/3 in 115 overs in the third innings. They had been reduced to 13/3 in 6.2 overs before recovering.The result further affected India's chances of qualifying for the World Test Championship final. Their points percentage dropped from 51.52 to 50, although they remained fourth in the standings. New Zealand slipped from second to third with 66.67 per cent.South Africa continued to lead the table with 75 per cent, while Australia moved up to second place with 69.23 per cent.There was a strong breeze and some cloud cover during the day, but the pitch remained easy for batters to play on. New Zealand's batters were able to defend and play through the line without having to deal with uneven bounce. Mitchell and Phillips, both known for their white-ball batting, showed their defensive skills as Gill rotated his bowlers without finding a breakthrough.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Not at peak': Shubman Gill opens up on Mohammed Siraj's omission from first Test vs New Zealand
articles.summary: India captain Shubman Gill has opened up about the decision to leave Mohammed Siraj out of the playing XI for the opening Test against New Zealand at the
articles.body: India captain Shubman Gill has opened up about the decision to leave Mohammed Siraj out of the playing XI for the opening Test against New Zealand at the Basin Reserve in Wellington. Gill admitted that dropping the experienced fast bowler was a difficult decision but said the team picked its players based on current form.Siraj's absence attracted attention, given his importance to India's pace attack. He has been India's leading wicket-taker in the ongoing World Test Championship cycle, with 43 wickets in 11 Tests.India opted for a four-man pace attack, with Jasprit Bumrah, Akash Deep, Prasidh Krishna and Anshul Kamboj making the playing XI. Washington Sundar was picked as the specialist spinner, while Siraj and Ravindra Jadeja were left out.Gill said the team had discussed the combination at length before taking the call. He also acknowledged Siraj's performances in the preceding ODI series.Gill revealed that he had spoken to Siraj personally before the match to explain the decision."Siraj’s a really good friend and dropping him was a really tough call. We have played lot together and I know him since early days. I had a chat with him before the Test explaining him the call, and he understood that," Gill told reporters after the first Test ended in a draw."See every player will see a phase where they are not at their peak, and we picked on current form," he said.Gill backs India's team combinationIndia's decision to leave out Siraj and Jadeja also came under scrutiny after New Zealand's batters put up a strong resistance to save the opening Test.When asked whether the accuracy of Siraj and Jadeja could have made a difference, Gill disagreed."Could Jadeja and Siraj’s accuracy made the difference? “I don’t think so,” asserts GillMitchell, Phillips frustrate India to secure drawDaryl Mitchell and Glenn Phillips put up a determined fight as New Zealand held India to a draw in the opening Test on Monday.New Zealand resumed the final day at 119/2, still 233 runs behind India's first-innings total. India struck twice in the morning session, dismissing overnight batters Devon Conway (65) and Rachin Ravindra (37). Washington Sundar and Prasidh Krishna picked up the wickets.Anshul Kamboj then dismissed Tom Blundell (15 off 54 balls), but that proved to be India's only success in the second session as New Zealand continued to resist.India also missed a run-out opportunity when Akash Deep failed to collect the ball cleanly, giving Mitchell a lifeline.The New Zealand batter made full use of the reprieve and remained unbeaten on 49 off 186 balls. Phillips, who had scored a century in the first innings, also stayed unbeaten, making 26 off 126 deliveries.The two batters faced 259 balls together to help New Zealand finish at 239/5 in 120 overs and secure a draw.Earlier, India had declared their first innings at 702/9 after bowling out New Zealand for 368.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.summary: India's bowlers put in a long effort on the final day of the first Test against New Zealand, but the pitch at the Basin Reserve offered little help as the
articles.body: India's bowlers put in a long effort on the final day of the first Test against New Zealand, but the pitch at the Basin Reserve offered little help as the hosts held on for a draw in Wellington on Monday. Daryl Mitchell and Glenn Phillips batted through the final session to ensure New Zealand finished their second innings at 239/5 before the two captains agreed to shake hands.India had started the day hoping to take eight wickets, with New Zealand resuming at 119/2. However, Mitchell remained unbeaten on 49 off 187 balls, while Phillips made 26 not out off 126 deliveries as the hosts resisted India's attack.The result was only the second drawn Test at the Basin Reserve in 15 matches since 2015. The other came in December 2018, when Sri Lanka, after conceding a 296-run first-innings lead, finished at 287/3 in 115 overs in the third innings. They had been reduced to 13/3 in 6.2 overs before staging their fightback.The draw has also affected India's chances of qualifying for the World Test Championship final. Their points percentage fell from 51.52 to 50, although they remained fourth in the standings. New Zealand slipped from second to third with a points percentage of 66.67.South Africa continued to lead the table with 75 per cent, while Australia moved up to second place with 69.23 per cent.There was a strong breeze and some cloud cover throughout the day, but the pitch remained easy to bat on. The New Zealand batters were able to play their shots and defend without having to deal with uneven bounce. Mitchell and Phillips, both known for their white-ball batting, showed their defensive skills as India captain Shubman Gill kept rotating his bowlers but could not find a way through.Second consecutive draw for IndiaThis was India's second consecutive drawn Test and further affected their chances of reaching the World Test Championship final. Earlier in August, India had drawn the second Test against Sri Lanka at the SSC in Colombo after enforcing the follow-on.The last time India had played two or more consecutive drawn Tests was more than a decade ago. They had three draws in a row during the 2014-15 tour of Australia, against Australia in Melbourne and Sydney, followed by a draw against Bangladesh in June 2015.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Shubman Gill's straight talk: Mohammed Siraj dropped on form, calls out saliva ban and lifeless pitch at Basin Reserve
articles.summary: WELLINGTON: Shubman Gill didn't hold back when he was asked whether Ravindra Jadeja and Mohammed Siraj's accuracy could have made a difference at Basin
articles.body: WELLINGTON: Shubman Gill didn't hold back when he was asked whether Ravindra Jadeja and Mohammed Siraj's accuracy could have made a difference at Basin Reserve. He bluntly said, "I don't think so." Right before the query, the India captain had explained at length why Siraj wasn't considered for the Playing XI in the series opener and asserted how current form played a major part in the "very tough decision"."Siraj is a great player and a great bowler that has done very well for India. Before all of that, he's a really good friend of mine. We made our debuts together. Even before playing for India, we were really good friends. So leaving him behind was actually a very tough decision for him and for me as well. But sometimes you have to see which bowlers are in the form, which bowlers are bowling the best."I told him before the match that he's going to be missing out this match. And I don't know if he agreed or not, but he understood that. He understood what was the logic behind it. He understood why we picked someone else ahead of him. And I think in every player's career or life, there comes a phase where you're not going to be at the peak of your career all the time. And I think he understands that," Gill told reporters after the first Test between India and New Zealand ended in a draw on Day 5.Siraj's exclusion was the hottest topic across platforms for the last few days, and it gathered more steam after the result didn't go India's way. Gill, however, seemed absolutely convinced with the call he made. India controlled most periods of play in the Test, but New Zealand's resistance on the final day denied them a win.Teams should be allowed to use saliva. It was a rule that was made effective during COVID. I think we are long past that.The Indian captain's explanation regarding Siraj wasn't the only straightforward comment of the day, as he minced no words in calling out the quality of the ball and the saliva ban. Gill highlighted that it was an issue in England last year too."Teams should be allowed to use saliva. It was a rule that was made effective during COVID. I think we are long past that," said Gill."If you're not shining the ball or if you're not able to maintain the ball well, especially on wickets like these, it makes the job of the bowler very difficult. And also, the condition of the balls has not been too great lately. We had the same problem in England as well. We understand, after 50 overs, the ball will obviously go soft. But if the ball is going soft after 25-30 overs or it's going out of shape and you're also not able to maintain the ball and use saliva, then it's a very difficult job for the bowlers," he added.'Not a great Test wicket'India have had to settle for draws in their last two Tests, against Sri Lanka in Colombo and New Zealand in Wellington, and on both occasions, the pitches offered no assistance to the bowlers. India toiled hard and long to take the remaining five New Zealand wickets, but the moment it didn't look possible, the hands were shaken to settle for a draw. Basin Reserve is famous for being a fast bowler's paradise, but the conditions were a stark contrast to what one had expected in the build-up, especially after the lushness on the opening day.Yes, the clear skies and bright sunshine played their part, but the moment the pitch turned from green to brown, and factoring in the quality of the ball, the edges stopped carrying. Both teams resorted to keeping the wicketkeeper up, aiming for an LBW or bowled dismissal, as conventional edged-and-gone dismissals seemed highly unlikely.When we started playing the Test match, we thought there will be a lot more in the wicket. I think on Day 3, 4 and 5, it just went flatter and flatter."When we started playing the Test match, we thought there will be a lot more in the wicket. I think on Day 3, 4 and 5, it just went flatter and flatter. There were no scallops in the wicket. There was no impact of the overs being bowled on the wicket, or even the days being played. The wicket just got slower. So having seen that, I think it was not a great Test wicket, especially if you want results. But having said that, like I said before, now because we talk about results a lot more because of the WTC, before, draws were a lot more common. So people didn't talk about draws as much," said Gill.India's bowlers collectively sent down 241 overs in the match, and even though they didn't earn the crucial World Test Championship points, captain Gill was very pleased with the group's energy and body language. With just three days between the two games, one of which is a travel day, the Indian team has cancelled its team activity before the Christchurch fixture and hopes to recharge and refresh as its hunt for crucial points continues.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 'My silence should never be mistaken for weakness': Prithvi Shaw warns of legal action
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Prithvi Shaw has hit back at former cricketer Yograj Singh over his remarks about the batter's career and personal life.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Prithvi Shaw has hit back at former cricketer Yograj Singh over his remarks about the batter's career and personal life. Shaw said he had nothing to hide about his past but would not allow anyone to use it to spread negativity, damage his reputation or gain publicity.Yograj had blamed Shaw's career decline on his lifestyle, including partying, drinking and being in bad company. He also compared the Indian batter's situation with that of former India cricketer Vinod Kambli."Why did Prithvi Shaw go downhill? It happened with Vinod Kambli before him. It was because of parties, womanising, cigarettes, and drinking. I once asked Kambli, ‘What are you, son?’ You have so much talent," Yograj said on Sports Launchpad."You are coming to your room at 2.30 in the night. He said, ‘Your days are over, and we’re playing a different kind of cricket now.’ The next morning, Courtney Walsh bowled him, and India lost the match. Then the girl he was with left him, and no one offered him cigarettes and alcohol. The same happened with Shaw. When you go to parties, womanise, drink, and are in bad company, the same will happen to you as happened to them," he added.Shaw warns of legal actionShaw responded to Yograj's comments through a detailed Instagram statement. The batter said he had no issues with his past but would not accept attempts to target him or spread false claims about his personal life."My past is a part of my life, and I have absolutely nothing to hide or be ashamed of. However, I will not tolerate individuals deliberately using my name, my personal life, or my past to spread negativity, create unnecessary controversy, damage my reputation, or gain publicity and attention at my expense. There is a clear difference between expressing an opinion and deliberately targeting someone with false, misleading, defamatory, or malicious content. Let this be a clear and final warning: Any individual or platform engaging in such activities may face appropriate legal action," Shaw said.The batter also said he was ready to take legal steps to protect his dignity, privacy and reputation. He made it clear that his silence should not be mistaken for weakness."I reserve the right to pursue all legal remedies available to protect my dignity, privacy, and reputation. My silence should never be mistaken for weakness. I choose to move forward with dignity, but I will not hesitate to stand up for myself," he added.Shaw last represented India in 2021. The 27-year-old has played five Tests, six ODIs and one T20I for India.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: India-Pakistan cricket fans want ‘dirty politics’ kept out of beloved sport
articles.summary: Cricket’s die-hard fans say players are being forced to take part in acts of aggression for the benefit of politicians.
articles.body:
Doha, Qatar – Heated exchanges, scowling faces, body shoves, handshake controversies and trophy ceremony boycotts .

Cricket fans from India and Pakistan are no strangers to seeing their teams throw childlike tantrums on the field. Some even believe it’s the fire that fuels sport’s fiercest rivalry .

On Sunday, when the nations met in the Asia Cup Rising Stars 2026 in Doha, the temperature on the pitch matched the typically hot Middle Eastern afternoon.

Not long after Pakistan opted to bat first, India’s fast bowler Harshit Rana and Pakistan’s top-order batters were involved in what did not seem like a friendly exchange. Verbal blows were exchanged and dismissed batters were given hostile send-offs.

The trend continued during India’s innings, which ended 48 runs short of the target, giving the Pakistanis a rare victory over their neighbours.

In the stands, though, the supporters were following a different script.

It took a few hours for the West End International Cricket Stadium to fill up – with Sunday being the first working day of the week in Qatar – but towards the second half of the match, the attendance came close to its 10,000-person capacity.

Supporters of both countries, as well as neutral cricket fans, mingled in the stands while wearing their respective teams’ shirts, waving their own countries’ flags and chanting their players’ names.

For many, such as Abrar Hussain and Mohammed Saeed Khan, there didn’t seem to be a need for segregation while watching a sport both nations follow with equal fervour.

“We have been friends for over six years,” Khan told Al Jazeera.

Wearing a replica blue shirt of the Indian team, Khan sat next to his Pakistani friend Hussain, dressed in Pakistan’s shirt.

“We share accommodation, meals and a love for the game that goes beyond any rivalry,” the man from India’s southern port metropolis of Mumbai explained.

Khan and Hussain, who are teammates in a weekend cricket league in Doha, expressed their disappointment at the “politicisation of the sport.”

“Politics should stay out of the game,” said Hussain, a native of Pakistan’s largest city, Karachi.

“The game of cricket is very close to our heart. We don’t want anything spoiling our game.”

Recent cricket encounters between the two nations – at all levels, from senior men’s teams to women’s sides, as well as age-group teams – have been heavily politicised following their intense four-day conflict last May.

Four months after both countries returned from the brink of all-out war, their cricket teams met in the Men’s Asia Cup 2025 and seemed to carry the bitterness of the conflict onto the field.

India’s players avoided shaking hands with Pakistanis, who made gestures linked to the cross-border aerial fight. The tournament ended with the victorious Indian team refusing to accept the trophy from the Pakistani head of the Asian Cricket Council.

The pattern has followed every India-Pakistan cricket encounter and even found its way into the Under-19 Asia Cup, where Indian players’ behaviour after sealing a win was heavily criticised.

Indian cricket fan Khan believes many players don’t want to partake in such aggression but are “forced into the act” at the behest of politicians and the younger generation is following suit.

“Cricket boards should take disciplinary action against [such] players and ensure that this behaviour is not passed on to the next generation.”

Khan’s teammate and good friend, Hussain, agreed.

“It is a worrying sign for the sport,” he said of the on-field antics.

“Politics has poisoned cricket and the fact that young cricketers show this behaviour is not good for the future of the game.”

The venue for the tournament in Qatar is in the heart of Asian Town, a Doha suburb inhabited by migrants from South Asia who work in the capital’s Industrial Area.

For several thousand workers, a tournament bringing their home nations to their neighbourhood is a welcome change from the everyday grind of their work lives.

To have these matches a short walk away from their accommodation is an added bonus.

However, the lure of an India-Pakistan cricket match brought fans from across the Gulf state.

Doha resident Avinash Daniel, originally from India’s capital New Delhi, brought along his young family and two friends after hearing about the fixture.

“It’s our first time watching an India-Pakistan match at a stadium and it’s been a great experience,” Daniel said.

Sweeping his gaze around the stand, he pointed out that a mix of Indian and Pakistani fans surrounded his group but they were happily mingling with each other.

“There are no different sides in the stands,” he said with a shrug. “No Indian stands, no Pakistani stands. We are all mixed. It’s a wonderful cultural experience.”

Daniel, a railway engineer, believed the politicisation of cricket only benefits politicians, not cricketers or fans, who only want to enjoy the sport that offers a brief respite to its billions of fans.

“At the end of this match, both Indians and Pakistanis will go out and eat the same mandi – a traditional Arab rice and meat dish – probably cooked and served by Indians and Pakistanis.”

articles.title: Sandpapergate: AB de Villiers makes explosive claim about ball-tampering in 2018 Durban Test
articles.summary: AB de Villiers weighed in on Sandpapergate claiming he has "zero per cent doubt" that the entire Australian team knew ball tampering was taking place during their 2018 tour of South Africa; the former Proteas batter claimed ball tampering was taking place in the first Test
articles.body:
The former South African batter, who featured throughout the 2018 series, has also backed Usman Khawaja and Cameron Bancroft's explosive revelations about Sandpapergate, claiming that Australia's bowlers "knew" about the ball-tampering operation .

"It started in Durban, by the way, not in PE [Port Elizabeth]," de Villiers said on his YouTube channel, AB de Villiers 360.

"And I'm very happy for people to quote me on that. We lost that first Test match in Durban with the ball reversing at a very, very interesting time. Way too early for anyone to reverse a ball at Kingsmead.

"Trust me, I've played a lot of cricket there. So whatever they did there, whether it was sandpaper or a nail or I don't care. I honestly do not care. The fact of the matter is they were caught and everyone knew.

"The bowlers in particular knew because the ball doesn't just reverse.

"It's not your first Test match for Australia. So just stand up and say, 'guys, we were wrong'."

The controversy was reignited earlier in November following the publication of Khawaja's autobiography, Sabr , in which the former opening batter wrote that every member of the Australian side knew ball tampering was taking place.

David Warner, Chadd Sayers and Bancroft all supported that claim. However, under-fire Australian Test captain Pat Cummins denied the allegations as "100 per cent wrong" during an extraordinary press conference.

Darren Lehmann, who coached Australia during the series, later followed Cummins telling BBC Test Match Special : "I did not know sandpaper was being used."

Bowlers Josh Hazlewood, Nathan Lyon, Mitchell Starc and Cummins had issued a statement in 2021 again denying any use of Sandpaper during the series, and Hazlewood has since criticised the "pile on" against Cummins .

'Every single person knew, I have zero per cent doubt'

De Villiers featured in all four Test matches during the 2018 series and was at the crease alongside Aiden Markram when Bancroft was caught by TV cameras pulling a piece of sandpaper out of his pocket during the third Test.

In Durban, De Villiers struck an unbeaten 71 in the first innings, lifting his side to a 118-run win over South Africa, before going on to score an unbeaten 126 in the second Test in Port Elizabeth.

"It's the weirdest thing because everyone's talking about the sandpaper now," De Villiers added.

"Why are we all so worried about the object that was used?"

"The fact of the matter is there was a premeditated decision made to do something illegal on the ground.

"And every single person knew about it. I have zero per cent doubt about it."

De Villiers: Cricket Australia needs to take responsibility

While Cummins has been facing scrutiny over his position as Australia's Test captain in the wake of Khawaja and Bancroft's explosive revelations, Cricket Australia has now thrown it's "unanimous support" behind the fast bowler .

Cricket Australia has ruled out the prospect of re-opening an investigation into Sandpapergate, but has instead opened an independent forum , inviting former players to share their recollections of the scandal, without fear of punishment.

"We believe this is in the best interests of the game," Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg said.

"For almost a decade, the fallout from those events has remained part of the conversation around Australian cricket."

Following Cricket Australia's initial investigation, Warner and Steve Smith were both handed 12-month bans for ball tampering, while Bancroft was issued with a nine-month suspension, and De Villiers said that their punishments were too great.

De Villiers said the team threw those three players "under the bus", adding it was "absolutely ridiculous" how they "took the hit" and added their punishments were "too much".

Sky Sports has contacted Cricket Australia for comment.

After Khawaja's autobiography was published, Cricket Australia released a statement saying it remained "comfortable with the findings of our integrity process."

However, De Villiers believes the governing body needs to take responsibility for the saga.

"I think Cricket Australia need to take the blame and not so much the players because they didn't deal with it in the right manner," he said.

De Villiers added: "It should have been dealt with a lot better by the guys at the top, not the players.

"The players obviously panicked. They were emotional, in the middle of a series, in the middle of a Test match.

"They had no idea how to deal with it. I just feel they should have stuck together as a unit. They threw the guys under the bus and forced a situation like this to pop up again eight years later."

Former England captain Sir Andrew Strauss has broken his silence on the sandpaper revelations and threw his backing behind Australia Test captain Pat Cummins.

In a post on LinkedIn , Strauss said it was "time to let go" but added "the truth was always going to come out eventually."

"I cannot help feeling that it is time for everyone to get off their high horse," Strauss wrote. "For all the wrongs committed in Australian cricket, plenty of people seem rather too happy to jump on the bandwagon and revel in the soap opera. This all happened a long time ago. Punishments were handed out, reputations suffered and, one hopes, lessons were learnt.

"We seem increasingly prone to expressing mock outrage whenever someone does something wrong, all too eager to pass judgement from a position of sanctimonious righteousness. There is a place for accountability, but there should also be room for perspective, forgiveness and moving on.

"Cummins should not be made to carry the can for the actions of a previous regime. At some point, we have to draw a line under the past and move forward."

articles.title: 'I had no idea RCB would retain me': Yash Dayal on franchise's faith after a difficult year
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Expressing his gratitude to Royal Challengers Bengaluru, who recently kept faith in him by confirming his retention at Rs 5 crore on Nov 17 as
articles.body: MUMBAI: Expressing his gratitude to Royal Challengers Bengaluru, who recently kept faith in him by confirming his retention at Rs 5 crore on Nov 17 as part of a 20-player core, despite his troubles in the last one year, Yash Dayal has promised to give it his all to his franchise in IPL- 2027."It's a very big thing for me. I had no idea that the RCB would retain me. The RCB retained me and showed faith in me. So, I will try my best to do well for them. With whatever experience I have, I will try my 100 % to do my best this season," Dayal told TOI in an interview on Sunday night, soon after taking two for 29 in four overs to play a key role in Uttar Pradesh's 12-run win over defending champions Jharkhand in the Syed Mushtaq Ali T20 Trophy.The left-arm pace bowler had taken 13 wickets in 15 matches at 36.15, at an economy rate of 9.59, contributing well in RCB's maiden title triumph in 2025, but had to miss out playing in IPL-2026 after being entangled in a couple of legal cases.Dayal naturally badly missed playing cricket in what was surely the most difficult phase of his life. "Obviously, when you have your own players and watch matches on TV, it feels bad to sit at home. But it's okay. I can play now," he said.Dayal is understandably relishing playing again in domestic tournaments for UP. "Yes, I am enjoying it. I just want to play cricket. Cricket is everything for me. I don't care if I win or lose. My performance doesn't matter. I just want to enjoy my life, and cricket is my life," the fast bowler stressed.Dayal still hasn't given up on his dream to wear the India cap one day. "My ultimate goal is to represent India. I am 28 years old. I want to play for India as soon as possible. I want to forget all the years that I have missed. So, I just want to make it happen, no matter how long it isDuring a tumultuous phase in his life, Dayal married social media influencer Shweta Pundir. The left-arm quick said that marriage has made him concentrate more on cricket now. "I have become well-centered. I am trying to focus only on the game," he said.After missing out on a season of cricket due to legal cases against him that have been reportedly closed, Dayal looks intent to make up for lost time.In the four matches that he has played in the Syed Mushtaq Ali T20 Trophy for Uttar Pradesh, the left-arm fast bowler has picked up six wickets at 22.66, with an economy rate of 9.71.On Sunday, Dayal provided fine support to veteran seamer Bhuvneshwar Kumar, who took three for 39, to help UP pull off a win over Jharkhand"Overall, I bowled well. In the beginning, I was trying to pitch the ball a little ahead, but it wasn't happening that way. But as I was discussing with Kuldeep (Yadav) and Bhuvibhai, whatever you have to plan at the last minute, there should be clarity in it. So, I executed that clarity and it felt good," Dayal analysed.The seamer, who has taken 72 wickets in 75 T20 matchesat30.09, with an economy rate of 8.76, is learning a lot while bowling in tandem with 'swing king' Bhuvneshwar in SMAT. "When you are standing at the other end, or fielding somewhere, you see his field settings, what line is bowling, what shots the batters are hitting (off his bowling) you get to learn a lot from that. He has a lot of experience," Bhuvneshwar said.Years of success in the IPL-he has played 43 matches for Gujarat Titans and then RCB, in which he has taken 41 wicketsat33.90, at an economy rate of 9.57, has clearly helped Dayal understand what is required to survive as a bowler in this format. "I am still learning. I can't say that I have become very smart. I just focus on the changes I have to make match by match and according to the format," Dayal said.Bowling for RCB at ground with small dimensions like the Chinnaswamy Stadium in Bengaluru is not an easy task, but Dayal takes it as "challenge.""It's tough to bowl on small grounds like the Chinnaswamy and the Wankhede Stadium. You have to see where the batsman is playing the shot. Where can I bowl? What field can I take? Different grounds have different experiences. I have tried to apply what is required at the Chinnaswamy Stadium as a bowler. When you take the ball and mark your run up, you see that the boundary is close to you. So it is difficult to save runs. But I enjoy that challenge a lot," explained the pacer.Dayal is constantly looking to evolve as a bowler. "I have worked on overall lengths. I have worked on my yorker, bouncer and the length Ball. I am also working on my slower delivery. I am also thinking about what else I can produce," he said.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: AB De Villiers: Former South Africa batter claims Australia were ball-tampering from first Test of 2018 series
articles.summary: Former South Africa batter AB de Villiers says "there is absolutely no doubt in my mind" that Australia were altering the ball from the opening Test in 2018.
articles.body:
Former South Africa batter AB de Villiers has alleged Australia were ball-tampering from the first match of their controversial 2018 Test series.

Australia captain Steve Smith, vice-captain David Warner and batter Cameron Bancroft received long-term bans for their roles in using sandpaper to alter the ball during the third Test in Cape Town.

Former Australia batter Usman Khawaja, whose new autobiography has re-started scrutiny of the scandal, has previously claimed that sandpaper was also used during the preceding Test at Gqeberha, then known as Port Elizabeth.

Warner and Bancroft have both corroborated Khawaja's claims about that match, but De Villiers has now suggested the ball was altered during the series opener in Durban.

"It started in Durban, by the way, not in PE," De Villiers said on his YouTube channel ABD360. "I'm very happy for people to quote me on that.

"I see everyone is sort of admitting that in Port Elizabeth it also happened. I can very much tell you Durban was no different, in the first Test. Go look at the footage. Absolutely no doubt in my mind.

"We lost that first Test match in Durban with the ball reversing at a very, very interesting time. Way too early for anyone to reverse a ball at Kingsmead. Trust me, I've played a lot of cricket there.

"So whatever they did there, whether it was sandpaper or (a) nail, I don't care. The fact of the matter is they were caught and everyone knew. Just stand up and say 'we were wrong'. A lot is at stake now because they lied.

"The bowlers in particular knew because the ball doesn't just reverse. It's not your first Test match for Australia. So just stand up and say, 'guys, we were wrong'."

In a 4,000-word article last week, Bancroft said sandpaper wasn't used in Durban, where left-arm paceman Mitchell Starc finished with match figures of 9-109 as he bowled Australia to their one victory in the series.

"Casting forward to the first Test in Durban, sandpaper was not used," he wrote. "There were more traditional methods of maintaining the ball, including saliva. I cannot say with certainty whether mints or lollies were involved. Probably quarter-seam picking, this practice became so normal after my first Test."

Australia's bowling attack in the three Tests and Darren Lehmann, their head coach at the time, have consistently denied any knowledge of ball-tampering during the series.

Current Test captain Pat Cummins, who was part of the bowling attack, labelled Khawaja's claims as "100% wrong" and "utter nonsense" at a news conference earlier this month and has received backing from Cricket Australia to continue in his role.

Cricket Australia has launched an independent "forum" for players and staff involved in the scandal to voluntarily share their version of events, but it is not a full investigation and will not involve any new penalties.

"It's become really personal for all the people involved and I do have sympathy for them," added De Villiers, who played in every match in the series and retired from international cricket after its conclusion.

"Obviously not sympathy for what took place on that day and who knows how many games before then.

"I just feel they should have stuck together as a unit. They threw the guys under the bus and forced a situation like this to pop up again eight years later."

De Villiers also acknowledged that he was not an "angel" during his playing career but insisted his side had stayed within the rules of the game when working on the ball.

"I'm not playing all innocent and saying that I'm the perfect person," he said. "We all try and get the ball to reverse. We try and bounce it in. We try and do it in a legal manner and we try and push the boundaries as much as possible.

"We all have tried over the years to get the ball to do something, to get an edge, but obviously not being as stupid as to take an object onto the field and blatantly cheating."

Cricket Australia has been contacted for comment.

articles.title: 'Where is Kuldeep Yadav or Manav Suthar?': Sourav Ganguly questions India's team selection after Wellington draw
articles.summary: Former India captain Sourav Ganguly has questioned India's decision to leave out specialist spinners Kuldeep Yadav and Manav Suthar from the playing XI
articles.body: Former India captain Sourav Ganguly has questioned India's decision to leave out specialist spinners Kuldeep Yadav and Manav Suthar from the playing XI for the first Test against New Zealand in Wellington. While praising India's batting performances in the opening Test of the two-match series, Ganguly stressed that having a genuine spinner is a must to win Test matches overseas, especially on pitches that become flatter as a match progresses.His comments came after India were held to a draw by New Zealand in the first Test at the Basin Reserve in Wellington. India had declared their first innings at a massive 720/9 and were in a strong position to push for victory, but could not take the remaining five wickets on the final day.New Zealand had resumed the day at 119/2, still 233 runs behind. However, the hosts showed great patience to finish at 239/5 after 120 overs. Captain Shubman Gill shook hands with the opposition batters with less than an hour left in the match.Daryl Mitchell remained unbeaten on 49 off 186 balls, while Glenn Phillips scored an unbeaten 26 off 126 deliveries. The pair batted patiently to keep India's bowlers at bay and secure a draw.In a post on X, Ganguly praised India's performances in both white-ball and red-ball cricket during the tour. However, he questioned the team's decision to play without a specialist spinner, naming Kuldeep Yadav and Manav Suthar.“India has been brilliant this series .. white ball and now red ball .. the batting application looked super .. but they must understand to win test matches away a genuine spinner is a must on pitches which get flat with time ..u have to play one in test cricket .. Washington can play as an allrounder ..@bcci where is Kuldeep or Manav sutar ?,” Ganguly wrote.Ganguly's comments highlighted the importance of having a specialist spinner alongside Washington Sundar, who played as an all-rounder. India went into the Wellington Test with four fast bowlers — Jasprit Bumrah, Prasidh Krishna, Akash Deep and Anshul Kamboj - while leaving out Ravindra Jadeja.The decision to leave out Jadeja also raised questions among cricket experts.Kuldeep was initially part of India's Test squad but was released to play domestic cricket. Gurnoor Brar was later added to the squad. Kuldeep had played the fourth ODI against New Zealand before the Test series, conceding 73 runs in his eight overs.Suthar, who made his Test debut against Afghanistan earlier this year, was also not part of the squad. He picked up seven wickets in that match and had earlier played an important role in India's 1-0 series win over Sri Lanka, taking 16 wickets across two matches.India also left out Mohammed Siraj from the playing XI for the Wellington Test.India will now face New Zealand in the second and final Test at Hagley Oval in Christchurch, starting November 27.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: IND vs NZ 1st Test: Tom Latham explains why New Zealand are 'happy' with Wellington draw despite India domination
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: New Zealand captain Tom Latham believes his team has earned a result that feels like a victory after managing to draw the first Test against
articles.body: NEW DELHI: New Zealand captain Tom Latham believes his team has earned a result that feels like a victory after managing to draw the first Test against India in Wellington on Monday. He said the draw was especially satisfying considering the difficult positions New Zealand found themselves in during the match.India declared their first innings at 720/9 but fell five wickets short of victory after Daryl Mitchell and Glenn Phillips put up a strong fight on the final day. The pair batted patiently for almost two sessions to keep India from taking the remaining wickets.The match going into the fifth day had looked unlikely after India reduced New Zealand to 70/5 shortly after lunch on the opening day. However, the pitch became easier for batting, allowing the hosts to recover and score 368 in their first innings."I guess that's one that we've probably got away with," Latham told reporters at Basin Reserve."Looking at the position we were in on day one, I think the amount of pressure that we were put under to then be in a position where we got 360 or 370... we were certainly pretty happy (with that)."Heading into the third innings, where there's only a couple of results at play, I think (it's great) the way those guys were able to apply themselves and stick to their plans for a long period of time, and ultimately get the draw."Latham highlights importance of WTC pointsLatham, who was dismissed for ducks in both innings by Jasprit Bumrah in the first over each time, said the draw could prove important in New Zealand's bid to reach the World Test Championship (WTC) final.New Zealand were at the top of the WTC standings when the Test began last week but were overtaken by defending champions South Africa. Monday's draw will see them drop another place to third, behind Australia.However, with the second Test against India in Christchurch still to come, followed by a tour of Australia and a home series against Sri Lanka, Latham believes his team has enough matches left to fight for one of the two places in the WTC final at The Oval in June."Draws become important as well," added the opener, who helped New Zealand beat India in 2021 to win the first WTC final."It's not necessarily over one series that you've got to play well. It's over a two-year period and it depends on how many games you've got."Obviously, we've got more games left than most teams... (and) hopefully, we'll give ourselves a chance throughout the next couple of months to be in that position."Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: New Zealand vs India: Black Caps hold on for draw despite tourists record score as Shubman Gill calls for end to saliva ban
articles.summary: Shubamn Gill has called for the ban on saliva to be lifted after India trudged to a draw in the first Test against New Zealand;  Daryl Mitchell and Glenn Phillips held firm for 43 overs Monday to earn the Black Caps a hard-fought draw after India posted a record score of 720-9d
articles.body:
A resolute partnership between Daryl Mitchell and Glenn Phillips held firm for 43 overs Monday to earn the Black Caps parity in the first instalment of the two-Test series, frustrating the high-flying tourists who declared on 720-9 on day four - the record score of any team in New Zealand.

The high-scoring affair led Gill to question why saliva has not been reinstated as a legitimate method to elicit swing, after the ban was introduced to reduce the spread of Covid-19 in 2020. Sweat is still a permitted method according to ICC regulations.

"I don't know why ball shining [using saliva] is not allowed," Gill said. "It's been years since the Covid-19 pandemic passed, I don't know why it's not allowed now."

New Zealand resumed at 119-2 on day five, giving India at least 90 overs available to capture the eight wickets it needed to take a series lead ahead of the second test in Christchurch from Friday.

New Zealand needed 233 runs to make India bat again but that thought was subordinated to the imperative of defence, to secure the draw that would keep the series alive.

Mitchell and Phillips are typically attacking batters but both suppressed that nature for the good of the team. Phillips scored 26 from 126 balls and Mitchell was 49 not out from 186 balls before the teams shook hands and stumps were drawn with an hour remaining in the day.

"We knew it was going to be a challenge to get 10 wickets on that pitch," Gill continued. "We had a couple of chances and a decent day in the field.

"We were impressive touring away from home and I think we challenged them in all areas."

New Zealand defence prevails despite India's record score

The feature of the match which will last longest in the memory will be India's mammoth first innings.

K.L Rahul made 136, putting on 130 for the first wicket with Yashasvi Jaiswal, who made 85. He then added 165 for the second wicket with Devdutt Padikka, who made 80, and 91 with Gill, who was out for 98 two balls before the end of Day 3.

India started well on the final day's play, capturing the wickets of the overnight batters Devon Conway and Rachin Ravindra in the first hour and the wicket Tom Blundell soon after lunch.

That brought together Mitchell and Phillips with New Zealand at 176-5 and with a long time left to secure a draw. Pressure was on both men as New Zealand's last specialist batting pair, with the bowling allrounder Nathan Smith to come in next, then the bowlers.

Phillips also played a key role in New Zealand's first innings with his innings of 118 in a partnership of 216 with Henry Nicholls which saved New Zealand's after it had been 70-5, sent in to bat on a green top.

Nicholls made 175 not out, guiding New Zealand to 368. The period in which they were together was the only period in the match in which New Zealand had the upper hand.

"As you look back over the five days from that first innings to where the game ended up, the wicket changed throughout but I thought it was a great test match," Nicholls said. "Both teams gave it everything.

"For us to get a draw from where we were was a pleasing result."

Wicketkeeper Pant then took over and compiled a dashing 128 from 153 balls in partnerships of 100 with Gill, 68 with nightwatchman Anshul Kamboj and 75 with Dhruv Jurel, who made 78.

Jasprit Bumrah, returning to test cricket after a 12 months absence, dismissed New Zealand captain Tom Latham in the first over of both innings.

The teams take four points each from the match toward the World Test Championship in which New Zealand is now third behind South Africa and Australia. India is fourth.

articles.title: 'I would like to ask Gill the logic behind that': Ex-cricketer questions India's captain after Wellington draw
articles.summary: Former India wicketkeeper-batter Dinesh Karthik has raised questions over Shubman Gill's captaincy, particularly his defensive field placements, after
articles.body: Former India wicketkeeper-batter Dinesh Karthik has raised questions over Shubman Gill's captaincy, particularly his defensive field placements, after India failed to force a result in the drawn first Test against New Zealand at the Basin Reserve in Wellington.India entered the final day needing eight wickets to secure a historic victory. However, they managed to dismiss only three New Zealand batters before the match ended in a draw. The hosts were largely comfortable during their second-innings resistance, with India creating very few genuine opportunities apart from a missed run-out chance and a half-chance that went Devdutt Padikkal's way at short leg.The prospect of making inroads with the new ball offered India their best chance of turning the game around. But the field placements continued to attract criticism, with Simon Doull and Sunil Gavaskar also questioning Gill's approach during the broadcast. India persisted with a fielder at cover instead of adding another player to the slip cordon or bringing in an extra close-in fielder.Karthik, too, was puzzled by the presence of boundary riders when India were searching for wickets despite having a substantial lead. He felt such placements could influence the bowlers' mindset and encourage the opposition to rotate the strike comfortably."I would like to ask Gill the logic behind that, having boundary riders in phases of play where you are looking to get wickets and when you don't mind boundaries being given. Even in Sri Lanka, there were times they had the boundary riders. The modern-day batter is quite comfortable with playing lofted shots, so you don't want to miss out on that, but they are also comfortable knocking around for singles when available. What is the mindset of the bowler when you have outfielders?" Karthik said on Cricbuzz.This is not the first time Gill has been unable to close out a Test after putting his team in a commanding position. India had faced a similar situation in Colombo against Sri Lanka, where they needed only a few more wickets to complete a 2-0 series sweep. However, Sonal Dinusha and the lower order held firm to secure a draw for the hosts.India had posted 720/9 declared in their first innings, but Karthik did not believe that declaring earlier would have made a difference to the outcome. In his assessment, the pitch was so heavily tilted in favour of batters that New Zealand could have survived even with more time available to them."I feel for him, I understand what he is saying as a skipper. I genuinely don't think that an early declaration would have helped. There was no correct time that they missed to declare. The pitch was so flat that New Zealand could have chosen to play another 60 overs and there was not much we could have done. The pitch was the villain. I don't think they declared wrong," Karthik concluded.The second Test between India and New Zealand will begin at Hagley Oval on Friday, November 27. Gill will be under pressure to turn things around as India continue to struggle in the 2025-27 World Test Championship standings. Their current points percentage stands at 50.00, leaving them well below the top two teams.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 148 balls for a hundred! Tilak Varma enters unwanted record books after India A's defeat to Pakistan A
articles.summary: Tilak Varma's century against Pakistan A in the Asia Cup Rising Stars tournament went into the record books, but for an unwanted reason, as the India A
articles.body: Tilak Varma's century against Pakistan A in the Asia Cup Rising Stars tournament went into the record books, but for an unwanted reason, as the India A captain registered the second-slowest hundred by an Indian batter in List A cricket.Tilak took 148 balls to reach his century, putting him behind only former India batter Manoj Prabhakar, who holds the record with a 151-ball hundred. The knock came during India's 48-run defeat to Pakistan A in a Group B encounter on Sunday.Chasing a challenging target of 314, India A were bowled out for 265 despite Tilak's hundred and an explosive 70 from Abhishek Sharma. While Tilak eventually reached the three-figure mark, his innings was a slow-burning effort, with his half-century itself taking 95 deliveries.The contrast between the two batters was evident from the beginning of the chase. Abhishek went on the offensive, smashing six fours and as many sixes in his 42-ball 70, while Tilak struggled to find his rhythm. At one stage, when Abhishek had raced to 60 off 34 balls, Tilak had managed just six runs off the same number of deliveries.Tilak's slow start put the middle order under pressure as the required run rate continued to climb. Abhishek's dismissal proved costly, with the remaining batters finding it difficult to maintain the scoring momentum against Pakistan's bowling attack.The India A captain eventually found some boundaries towards the latter stages of his innings and combined with Shahbaz Ahmed for a 112-run seventh-wicket partnership. Shahbaz contributed 56 off 41 balls, but his dismissal in the 43rd over left India with too much to do.India A eventually folded for 265 in 49.1 overs, falling 48 runs short of the target. Tilak's century, therefore, could not prevent his side from suffering defeat, while his scoring rate became a major talking point after the match.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 'MS Dhoni won't be involved in bidding': Irfan Pathan reveals what CSK legend will do at IPL 2027 auction
articles.summary: Former India pacer Irfan Pathan does not expect MS Dhoni to be part of Chennai Super Kings' (CSK) auction table when the franchise builds its squad for
articles.body: Former India pacer Irfan Pathan does not expect MS Dhoni to be part of Chennai Super Kings' (CSK) auction table when the franchise builds its squad for IPL 2027, insisting that the legendary wicketkeeper-batter will focus on his newly assigned mentoring responsibilities rather than the bidding process.The IPL 2027 auction is scheduled to take place in Goa on December 16.Dhoni's playing days in the IPL came to an end earlier this month after he communicated his desire to retire during a video call held to discuss CSK's player retentions for the upcoming season. He has since been appointed as the franchise's mentor.The former India captain featured for CSK in 17 of the 19 IPL seasons between 2008 and 2026. His only absences came in 2016 and 2017, when the franchise was suspended and he represented Rising Pune Supergiant.Pathan believes Dhoni will stay away from the auction proceedings, leaving recruitment decisions to the franchise's management and think tank. According to him, the five-time IPL-winning captain's responsibility will be to share his experience and help players succeed."Knowing Dhoni, I don't think he will be sitting at the auction table. He is the mentor, sitting at the auction table is not his role. His job is to guide the players, pass on his experience to them, help them perform and teach them how to win matches for CSK. The bidding and the auction decisions are left to the management," said Pathan on JioStar."He likes to keep things simple and let the people who know the job do it. CSK have a strong management and a think tank that have built title-winning squads for years, and Dhoni has always trusted them completely," said Pathan.Pathan also pointed out that Dhoni has traditionally preferred staying away from the spotlight when it comes to decisions taken away from the field. He expects the former captain to continue in the same manner, contributing to the franchise without being visibly involved in auction activities."So, I would be surprised if we see him sitting at CSK's auction table. He will be involved in his own way as a mentor, but it will be behind the scenes, not at the auction table," opined Pathan.Abhinav Mukund identifies CSK's biggest concern ahead of IPL 2027 auctionMeanwhile, former India batter Abhinav Mukund believes CSK need to address their bowling resources after their recent strategy of investing heavily in young players failed to deliver the desired results.The franchise has missed out on the playoffs in each of the last three seasons. Mukund felt that while some of their expensive acquisitions had struggled to make an impact, CSK also face a selection dilemma because of the number of Indian top-order batters in their squad."The gamble on youth hasn't paid off for CSK. Prashant Veer was bought for Rs 14.2 crore and didn't deliver, though you can't blame him much since he barely got to bowl. He's been released, so the money has come in," said Mukund.He also assessed the situation surrounding Kartik Sharma, another expensive acquisition who has retained his place in the squad."Kartik Sharma, the other 14-crore buy, played some match-winning knocks and has been retained. But CSK still have a surplus of Indian top-order batters. They can't fit Ruturaj Gaikwad, Sanju Samson, Ayush Mhatre, Dewald Brevis, Kartik Sharma, Urvil Patel and Sarfaraz Khan into one playing XI."Mukund believes CSK's bowling department requires the most attention at the auction. With several batting options already available, he suggested that the franchise could explore using its surplus batters in potential trades to acquire bowlers."Their main issue is the bowling. With Liam Livingstone's arrival, him, (Dewald) Brevis, and Noor Ahmad are sure starters, and the last overseas spot is likely Jamie Overton's. That makes it hard for Akeal Hosein and Noor to play together."CSK are looking for an Indian spinner, their bowling looks thin, but they have batters to offer. If a team wants to trade a bowler, CSK can give a batter in return and I can firmly see them bolstering their bowling at the auction," he added.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 'There was a time in my career when I was playing all three format': KL Rahul
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: KL Rahul has opened up about the challenges he faced while trying to balance Test cricket with the demands of ODIs and T20Is.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: KL Rahul has opened up about the challenges he faced while trying to balance Test cricket with the demands of ODIs and T20Is. The Indian batter admitted that switching between formats was not easy earlier in his career, as each required a different approach, mindset and preparation.Rahul recently made history with his 136-run knock against New Zealand at the Basin Reserve. He became the first Indian opener to score Test centuries in all four SENA countries (South Africa, England, New Zealand and Australia).He is also only the second Asian opener after Saeed Anwar to achieve the feat. His century was the first by an Indian batter in New Zealand in 12 years.Speaking in a video shared on bcci.tv, Rahul explained how experience and missed opportunities helped him understand the demands of Test cricket."There was a time in my career when I was playing all three format... I could not make that switch from trying to get bat on ball in T20 and ODI cricket to switching quickly in a week's time to leaving balls and trying to play as late as I possibly can, which is the basics of Test batting," said Rahul.Rahul on preparation and the demands of Test cricketThe 34-year-old said Test cricket requires patience, careful preparation and a different way of thinking compared to limited-overs formats.He compared his batting approach to his passion for making coffee, explaining how even a small mistake can affect the final result."Patience and the preparation, you get one tiny thing wrong and the (coffee) cup is going to taste bad. I think it's the same in Test cricket... one small mistake, one bad shot as a batter and your whole innings can mean nothing even if you've worked hard for three or four hours," he said.Rahul also revealed that he starts preparing mentally five or six months before challenging overseas tours, studying conditions and planning how to tackle them.Rahul opens up about injuries and missed opportunitiesDespite his historic century, Rahul said the achievement left him emotional and unable to sleep."Honestly, I've not slept at all the whole night and it's not because of excitement," he said.The batter also expressed disappointment over injuries that have interrupted his career, believing they may have cost him at least 10-15 Test appearances. Having played 71 Tests, Rahul hopes to remain fit, continue scoring runs and finish the final phase of his career strongly.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Rishabh Pant's seven SENA hundreds, one unusual Test record that refuses to change
articles.summary: Rishabh Pant's remarkable Test record in SENA countries has an interesting twist: despite scoring seven centuries across South Africa, England, New
articles.body: Rishabh Pant's remarkable Test record in SENA countries has an interesting twist: despite scoring seven centuries across South Africa, England, New Zealand and Australia, the wicketkeeper-batter is yet to be on the winning side in any of those matches.Pant's latest hundred, an unbeaten 128 against New Zealand in the opening Test in Wellington, helped him add another milestone to his already impressive Test career. However, India could not convert their commanding position into a victory, with New Zealand battling hard on the final day to secure a draw.Resuming the final day at 119/2, New Zealand were still 233 runs behind India's first-innings total of 702/9 declared. India managed to pick up three more wickets, with Washington Sundar, Prasidh Krishna and Anshul Kamboj striking, but Daryl Mitchell and Glenn Phillips frustrated the visitors with a resolute partnership.Mitchell remained unbeaten on 49 off 186 deliveries, while Phillips finished on 26 not out off 126 balls. The duo batted out 259 deliveries as New Zealand finished at 239/5 in 120 overs to salvage a draw.The result meant Pant's wait for a Test victory after scoring a century in a SENA country continued.Pant's seven Test centuries in SENA countriesScoreVenueResult114The OvalLost159*SydneyDrawn100*Cape TownLost146BirminghamLost134LeedsLost118LeedsLost128WellingtonDrawnDespite the unusual record, Pant's performances across these challenging overseas conditions underline his credentials as one of the finest wicketkeeper-batters in modern Test cricket.His latest hundred was his ninth in Test cricket, taking him past England's Les Ames for the third-most centuries by a designated wicketkeeper in the format. Only Australia's Adam Gilchrist (17) and Zimbabwe's Andy Flower (12) have scored more.Pant also became the sixth Indian batter to score a Test century in each of the four SENA countries (South Africa, England, New Zealand and Australia). Mohammad Azharuddin, Sachin Tendulkar, Rahul Dravid, Virat Kohli and KL Rahul are the other Indians to achieve the feat.Saeed Anwar, Younis Khan and Kumar Sangakkara are among the other subcontinental batters in this exclusive group.What makes Pant's achievement even more special is that he is the only batter on this list to have scored centuries in all four SENA countries as a designated wicketkeeper.At an age when a significant portion of his Test career still lies ahead, Pant has already established himself among the most prolific wicketkeeper-batters in the format. articles.title: Katie George: The tearaway quick reinvented as a top-order batter
articles.summary: Katie George was once a tearaway fast bowler but, after years of injury pain, tells BBC Sport about reinventing herself as a top-order batter.
articles.body:
Sportspeople are faced with a question when injuries hit again and again. Do I try one more time or should I walk away?

England's Katie George came really close to choosing the latter option last year.

"I had a couple of conversations with my close family and partner about whether it was taking too much out of me and whether I was happy with the person I was," she says. "I was pretty miserable."

George made her England debut in 2018 aged 18 as a tearaway fast bowler. She was quick. Some coaches believed generationally so.

She played seven internationals between March and July before the injuries first hit that summer. George is matter of fact about how many have followed. The list is enough to make the rest of us wince.

"Nine stress fractures in my back," she says. "I tore the cartilage off my rib.

"Bits and bobs. Ankle surgery. I have missed a lot of cricket."

Unable to bowl because of her back and little more than a tailender with the bat, George got into sides purely for her athleticism and a penchant for stunning catches. She was occasionally referred to as a 'specialist fielder'.

The label was meant as a compliment, but it still stung. She says she felt like an "empty uniform".

"For a long time I was worried about being the [injury prone ex-Liverpool and England striker] Daniel Sturridge - what could have been, all of that talent wasted," says George, who played football for Portsmouth in her youth.

"I found that really difficult. I didn't want to be that person.

"Over a period of time you get told you are really resilient and you have been through so much. Then when it keeps happening there is pressure and it gets harder.

"You need to look brave and be resilient and show less emotion than you are feeling. Anyone knows when you bottle that up it can get quite tricky."

Then came George's end-of-year appraisal at Warwickshire - that uncomfortable question. Quit or change something. George opted the latter.

Alongside coach Ali Maiden, an unlikely plan was hatched. George had more ducks than fifties at that point in her professional career but why not try and build on flashes of potential. Why not try and become a frontline batter?

"I always knew I was half decent at bowling but I never had that feeling for batting," she says.

"Right the way through age groups and my first fifty at Western Storm, there were moments where in a game it would come off but I would have no idea how to replicate it.

"I would always put it down to a fluke."

The turnaround has been extraordinary. Batting most regularly at number three, George topped the average tables for this season's One-Day Cup with a figure of 77.55.

A 98 against Blaze in April was followed by a first professional century against Lancashire in June. An unbeaten ton against Durham rounded off the campaign. She even opened in the T20 Blast.

"It is crazy it happened but there was a lot of hard work and I am very grateful to Ali," she says.

"He pushed me and challenged me as to why couldn't I change the narrative a little bit. I want to impact games.

"I don't want to sit on the bench. I can do that from my sofa."

As a result, George will travel to India for an England A tour that begins later this month.

She is there alongside youngsters tipped for bright futures but also established names like Lauren Filer and Tilly Corteen-Colman. Her partner Issy Wong was named in the squads but has withdrawn because of injury.

"We were doing a team thing a couple of weeks ago and we were asked what we are most proud of," George says.

"Until the last few months it probably would have been my England debut but, once I thought about it, it was actually being stood in that team room as a batter and wearing this kit again.

"If you said I would be here as a batter in England kit I would definitely have laughed and said you were smoking something."

Given her past, George would be wise not to look too far into the future. She has not given up on bowling again regularly, nor is she ready to listen to advice to stop.

Instead, she has been named Warwickshire captain for next season so will at least have the option to decide herself when to bowl.

Before then, England coach Charlotte Edwards, selector Lydia Greenway and England's new managing director of women's cricket Leah Poulton will all be in India for the upcoming tour, providing George the chance to impress.

"My dream would be to play a red-ball game for England," she says. "That is what I set out for do.

"It is what I watched as a kid with my dad. I vividly remember my first ever Test match watching Jimmy Anderson running in and bowling.

"Whether I am able to, I don't know. Maybe it will be as a batter - that would be the biggest plot twist ever."
